summary: A black-and-white spiral brick tower on Anastasia Island, built 1871-74 after the sea threatened the old Spanish-era tower, and now run by a maritime museum.

notes_for_editor: Evidence rests on the NRHP nomination, the USLHS roster and the museum's own history posts (which quote the keepers' logs) plus Lighthouse Friends (secondary, facts only). Pre-1891 Light-House Board reports are not in the local corpus and no newspapers were reachable (Chronicling America searches for FL 1874-1889 and 1880 returned nothing), so the 1870-1880 erosion, appropriations and ducks come via Lighthouse Friends. Conflicts left in the text: old tower fall (museum log 20 June 1880; Lighthouse Friends 22 Aug 1880; nomination 1880); lens year (1853 / 1854 / Wikipedia 1855); keepers house appropriation and finish (nomination 1872/1876; LHF 1874/1875); focal plane (nomination 101 ft; LHF 165 ft; record 49.1 m); county purchase of the house (nomination 1970, museum 1971); who removed the Civil War lens (Arnau and Nelligan per museum; Pacetti per LHF); William R. vs W. Russell; Frank Lovely appears in the nomination but not in the USLHS roster. The nomination also puts C. D. Daniels in 1936 (USLHS 1935). The LHB 1894 passage is cited by scan page 649 (printed page unverified); it describes a 150-ft tower. The Emerging Civil War blog (Oct 2026) was read but not used: it conflicts with the museum on Harn's appointment and mixes in Castle Pinckney keepers. Woolson's 1874 Harper's "The Ancient City" (cited by the nomination) is a fictionalised sketch and was not used as a record. The 1937 Bulletin says the first American lighthouse was established in 1824 and the present tower built in 1874 (columns interleaved in OCR; not cited). Today: hours and ticketing should be checked on the museum site. Fact-check 2026-10-22: removed the unsupported claim that the museum dates the county purchase to 1971 (museum and LHF say the county was about to buy).
